transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Bioinformatics tools & pipelines, for Tuesday, November 24.
Let's turn to Bioinformatics tools and pipelines, where today's theme is reproducible analysis at scale.

First, a Research Square preprint from the Wang lab benchmarks four callers for mitochondrial DNA variants from short-read genomes: MitoHPC, mtSwirl, mity and mtDNA-Server 2, using 1000 Genomes data and simulations across diverse haplogroups.

MitoHPC and mtSwirl performed best, especially in non-European populations, and MitoHPC is easier to set up. mity was best at low-frequency variants but weaker on indels. mtDNA-Server 2 was most sensitive but had more false positives.

The authors then built a workflow called MARVel on MitoHPC, adding quality control and interactive variant curation. In an ataxia cohort it recovered known pathogenic variants and flagged new candidates.
It's a preprint, and those candidates need validation, but the diverse benchmark makes it useful for large cohorts.

Next, a bioRxiv preprint from the Hitz lab describes the IGVF Data Portal. It holds over 240 terabytes of results on genomic variation and function, available through a browser, an API and agentic tools.
It's a resource paper, but for labs interpreting non-coding variants, it's a natural place to look for functional evidence.

Third, the Tully lab presents NanoHIV-DR, a Nextflow workflow for HIV drug resistance from Nanopore data. It runs from raw files to clinician-readable reports and detects mutations below the consensus.

The abstract reports no performance numbers, so accuracy still has to be shown. Nextflow is a recurring thread. In Nucleic Acids Research, the Finn lab's MGnify version 6 moves its microbiome pipelines to Nextflow and adds viral and mobilome annotation.
In the same journal, the Winkelman lab's VEuPathDB update reports over 2,600 datasets and containerized pipelines. It also describes surviving on community funding after losing its federal grant.
And in the Journal of Cell Science, the Naba lab's MatriSpace maps extracellular matrix gene expression in spatial transcriptomics, as an R package and a no-code web app.
The takeaway: containerized workflows and no-code tools are becoming standard, but you still need careful benchmarks like the mitochondrial one to know which tool to trust.
